Data and analysis from Census 2021

How the relationship between UK public sector monthly income and expenditure leads to changes in deficit and debt.

This is the latest release.
                View previous releases

Contact: Email Public Sector Finance Delivery team

Print this 
Statistical bulletin

Borrowing in October 2026 was slightly higher than last year, as public spending grew by more than income, partly because of higher debt interest costs.

Despite the increase in October, borrowing in the financial year to date remained lower than over the same period last year.

Debt continued to rise in cash terms, having passed £3 trillion for the first time in September 2026, and remained historically high as a proportion of the economy.

Figure 1: The UK borrowed £17.0 billion in October 2026, up £0.8 billion on the same month last year

Borrowing – the difference between total public sector spending and income – was £17.0 billion in October 2026; this was £0.8 billion (5.2%) more than in October 2025.

Central government debt interest payable was £11.2 billion in October 2026; this was £2.8 billion (33.4%) more than in October 2025.

Borrowing was £111.3 billion in the financial year (FY) to October 2026; this was £7.3 billion (6.1%) less than in the same period last year.

Borrowing in the FY to October 2026 was 3.5% of gross domestic product (GDP), 0.3 percentage points lower than in the same period last year but the 14th-highest April-to-October figure since monthly records began in 1993.

Public sector net debt – the amount owed to the UK private sector and overseas, less liquid assets – was provisionally estimated at £3,058.3 billion (£3.1 trillion) at the end of October 2026, £161.6 billion more than last year.

Debt at the end of October 2026 was equivalent to 95.8% of GDP, 1.9 percentage points higher than last year and at levels last seen in the early 1960s.

Public sector net financial liabilities – a wider balance sheet measure than net debt, which includes additional financial assets and liabilities – were provisionally estimated at £2,696.2 billion (£2.7 trillion) at the end of October 2026, £162.3 billion more than last year.

Net financial liabilities were 84.5% of GDP at the end of October 2026; this was 2.4 percentage points higher than last year but 11.3 percentage points lower than net debt, as the additional financial assets included exceed the additional financial liabilities.

Public sector borrowing was £17.0 billion in October 2026.

This was the third-highest October borrowing since monthly records began in 1993, behind those of 2024 and 2020 (not adjusted for inflation). This was £0.8 billion (5.2%) higher than last year and £0.8 billion above the March 2026 Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) forecast.

!
    
        Our initial estimates of borrowing for the most recent months are susceptible to revisions in later months. Estimates of public corporations' data including those of Bank of England and public sector pensions are highly provisional estimates.

Central government is the largest subsector of the public sector and the main contributor to monthly public sector borrowing.

Despite higher tax receipts, central government borrowing was £20.8 billion in October 2026, broadly unchanged from last year, when it was £0.1 billion higher.

The latest estimate is provisional and may be revised as more data become available.

Central government receipts were £93.6 billion in October 2026. This was £6.7 billion higher than in October 2025, with income-related taxes making the largest contribution to this increase.

The forecasts underlying our current tax estimates reflect the expectations published in the Economic and fiscal outlook – March 2026 report from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).

Our Public sector current receipts: Appendix D dataset provides a detailed breakdown of central government income.

Central government current expenditure was £99.3 billion in October 2026. This was £7.0 billion higher than in October 2025, with increases spread across spending on debt interest, public services, social benefits and other costs.

Source: Public sector finances from the Office for National Statistics

Central government borrowing is mainly financed by gilts issued by the Debt Management Office. The UK government then pays interest to the investors who hold these gilts.

Central government debt interest payable was £11.2 billion in October 2026, £2.8 billion more than in October 2025. This was the highest October figure since monthly records began in 1997 and only the ninth month on record in which interest payable exceeded £10.0 billion. These figures are not adjusted for inflation.

Interest payable on index-linked gilts changes with the Retail Prices Index (RPI), which can make monthly debt interest costs volatile. Of the £11.2 billion payable in October 2026, £4.2 billion was the inflation-related uplift on index-linked gilts. This mainly reflected the 0.6% increase in the RPI between July and August 2026.

The inflation-related uplift builds up over the life of an index-linked gilt and is paid when the gilt is redeemed. Figure 3 shows this uplift in light blue as it is accrued rather than when it is paid.

Figure 3: Recent movements in the Retail Prices Index added £4.2 billion to central government debt interest payable in October 2026

The central government current budget deficit was £9.7 billion in October 2026, £0.6 billion more than in October 2025. This is the amount central government needed to borrow to fund day-to-day activities.

The deficit is the difference between £99.3 billion of current expenditure and £93.6 billion of current receipts, after accounting for £3.9 billion of depreciation.

The current budget balance excludes borrowing for capital investment. It shows whether current receipts are enough to cover day-to-day public services, welfare and administration.

Our Public sector finances borrowing by subsector: Appendix R dataset presents central government current budget deficit as a component of the total public sector current budget deficit. It also provides an additional breakdown of its components.

One of the government's fiscal objectives is to achieve a surplus in the public sector current budget by the financial year ending March 2030. Further information is provided in Section 6: UK fiscal targets.
